stem: Which statement best describes a covalent bond?

options.content: The attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons.
options.rationale: Correct: the bond is an electrostatic attraction involving the shared pair.

options.content: The attraction between oppositely charged ions.
options.rationale: This is an ionic bond.

options.content: The attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons.
options.rationale: This is a metallic bond.

options.content: The transfer of a pair of electrons from one atom to another.
options.rationale: Transfer gives ions; a covalent bond involves sharing.

explanation: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and the pair of electrons shared between them.

stem: How many lone pairs of electrons are there in one molecule of carbon dioxide, $\ce{CO2}$?

options.rationale: Correct: two lone pairs on each oxygen atom; carbon has none.
Each oxygen has two lone pairs, so there are four in total.
The oxygen atoms each keep two non-bonding pairs.
Six would be correct if each O had three lone pairs, but each O shares two pairs with carbon.

explanation: O=C=O: each oxygen shares two pairs with carbon and keeps two lone pairs. Carbon uses all four outer electrons in bonding.

stem: Which species contains a coordinate (dative covalent) bond?

options.rationale: Ammonia has three ordinary N–H bonds and a lone pair, but no dative bond.
Correct: nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺.
Each C–H bond uses one electron from C and one from H.
Ethene has ordinary single and double covalent bonds.

explanation: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺: the N lone pair forms the fourth N–H bond.

stem: In the dimer $\ce{Al2Cl6}$, how many coordinate bonds are there, and which atom donates the electron pair in each?

options.content: two; an aluminium atom donates to a chlorine atom
options.rationale: Aluminium in AlCl₃ is electron-deficient; it accepts, not donates.

options.content: two; a chlorine atom donates to an aluminium atom
options.rationale: Correct: each bridging Cl donates a lone pair to the electron-deficient Al of the other unit.

options.content: one; a chlorine atom donates to an aluminium atom
options.rationale: Each AlCl₃ unit accepts one pair, so there are two coordinate bonds.

options.content: six; every Al–Cl bond is a coordinate bond
options.rationale: Only the two bonds from bridging chlorines to aluminium are dative.

explanation: Al in AlCl₃ has six outer electrons. A Cl of each unit donates a lone pair to the Al of the other: two coordinate bonds, giving each Al an octet.
hints: Which atom in AlCl₃ has only six outer electrons?

stem: Which molecule has an expanded octet (more than eight electrons around the central atom)?

options.rationale: BF₃ has only six electrons around boron: an incomplete octet.
N has eight electrons: three bonding pairs and one lone pair.
Correct: six bonding pairs, twelve electrons around sulfur.
O has eight electrons: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs.

explanation: Period 3 elements such as S and P can have more than eight outer electrons (SF₆, PCl₅); Period 2 elements cannot.

stem: Bromochloromethane, $\ce{CH2BrCl}$, is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which halogen is replaced first, and why?

options.content: chlorine, because the C–Cl bond is more polar than the C–Br bond
options.rationale: C–Cl is more polar, but polarity is not the deciding factor; bond strength is.

options.content: chlorine, because chlorine is the more electronegative halogen
options.rationale: Higher electronegativity makes C–Cl more polar but also stronger, so it is broken less easily.

options.content: bromine, because the C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond
options.rationale: Correct: the weaker bond breaks more easily; bond strength outweighs polarity.

options.content: bromine, because the C–Br bond is shorter than the C–Cl bond
options.rationale: C–Br is longer than C–Cl because bromine is the larger atom.

explanation: C–Br (280 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than C–Cl (340 kJ mol⁻¹), so the C–Br bond breaks first and bromide is replaced first, even though C–Cl is the more polar bond.
hints: Which matters more for these reactions: bond polarity or bond energy?

stem:
Statements about bonds between two carbon atoms:

1. C≡C is shorter than C=C.
2. C≡C has a larger bond energy than C=C.
3. C=C has exactly twice the bond energy of C–C.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.rationale: Statement 3 is wrong: 2 × 350 = 700, more than 610.
Statement 1 is correct and statement 3 is wrong.
Correct: C≡C 840, C=C 610, C–C 350 kJ mol⁻¹, so the C=C value is less than double.
Statement 2 is also correct: more shared pairs, stronger bond.

explanation: More shared pairs give shorter, stronger bonds. C=C (610) is less than 2 × C–C (700) because the second (π) bond is weaker than the first (σ).
hints: Check statement 3 with the data booklet values.

stem:
Statements about nitrogen monoxide, NO:

1. It has an odd number of electrons.
2. It is a free radical.
3. Both atoms have an octet of electrons.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.rationale: With 11 outer electrons, both atoms cannot have eight.
Statement 1 is correct and statement 3 is wrong.
Statement 2 follows from statement 1: an unpaired electron makes it a radical.
Correct: 5 + 6 = 11 outer electrons, so one is unpaired; an octet on both atoms is impossible.

explanation: N (5) + O (6) = 11 outer electrons: odd, so one is unpaired and NO is a radical. With an odd number of electrons, one electron must be unpaired, so both atoms cannot have complete octets.
hints: Add the outer electrons of N and O.

stem: How many electrons are shared between the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
explanation: A triple bond is three shared pairs: six electrons.
workedSolution: 1. A triple bond is three shared pairs: six electrons.

stem: Use the data booklet average bond energy of C–H (410 kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to break all the C–H bonds in one mole of methane, CH₄(g).
explanation: CH₄ has four C–H bonds: 4 × 410 = 1640 kJ per mole of methane.
workedSolution: 1. CH₄ has four C–H bonds: 4 × 410 = 1640 kJ per mole of methane.
hints: How many C–H bonds are in each molecule?

stem: The bond energy of N≡N is 944 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in J, needed to break the bond in **one** nitrogen molecule. ($L = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
explanation:
1. 944 kJ mol⁻¹ = 944000 J mol⁻¹.
2. Per molecule: 944000 ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.57 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. (Not converting kJ to J gives a value 1000 times too small.)
workedSolution:
1. 1. 944 kJ mol⁻¹ = 944000 J mol⁻¹.
2. Per molecule: 944000 ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.57 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. (Not converting kJ to J gives a value 1000 times too small.)
hints: Convert kJ to J, then divide by L.

stem: How many electrons are in the outer shell of phosphorus in PCl₅?
explanation: Five P–Cl bonding pairs: ten electrons around phosphorus, an expanded octet.
workedSolution: 1. Five P–Cl bonding pairs: ten electrons around phosphorus, an expanded octet.

stem: In the ammonium ion, the N–H bond formed by the coordinate bond is longer than the other three N–H bonds.
explanation: False. Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical to the others: all four N–H bonds have the same length and energy.

stem: Boron trifluoride, BF₃, has only six electrons in the outer shell of boron.
explanation: True. Boron has three outer electrons and forms three B–F bonds: six electrons, so BF₃ can accept a lone pair (e.g. from NH₃).

stem: Match each molecule or ion with a feature of its bonding.
explanation: N≡N; twelve electrons around S; O lone pair donated to H⁺; 5 + 6 + 6 = 17 outer electrons; C=C.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Going from F–F to I–I, the halogen-halogen bond becomes {{blank:a}} because the shared pair is {{blank:b}} from the nuclei. A C=C bond is {{blank:c}} than a C–C bond.

explanation: Larger atoms give longer bonds; more shared pairs give shorter, stronger bonds. (F–F is unusually weak, 158 kJ mol⁻¹, because of lone-pair repulsion in the very short bond.)

stem: Give the formula of the ion formed when a water molecule forms a coordinate bond to a hydrogen ion (type it as, for example, NH4+).
explanation: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (the oxonium or hydronium ion).

stem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, and explain how the coordinate bond forms.

points.description: N at the centre with four shared pairs to four H atoms; no lone pairs on N
One shared pair has both electrons from nitrogen (shown as two dots / two of the same symbol)
The ion is in square brackets with a + charge; the bond forms when the N lone pair is donated to H⁺ (which has an empty orbital)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nitrogen sits at the centre with four bonding pairs to four hydrogen atoms and no lone pair. Three pairs contain one electron from N and one from H; the fourth contains two electrons from nitrogen, because it formed when ammonia's lone pair was donated into the empty 1s orbital of H⁺. The whole ion is shown in square brackets with a + charge.

explanation: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ by donation of the lone pair.

stem: Explain why nitrogen, N₂, is much less reactive than chlorine, Cl₂. Use the bond energies N≡N 944 and Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹.

points.description: N₂ has a triple bond; Cl₂ has a single bond
N≡N bond energy (944) is much larger than Cl–Cl (242)
So reactions of N₂ have a high activation energy / much energy is needed to break the bond
N≡N is non-polar (and N₂ has no low-energy empty orbitals), so it is not attacked by nucleophiles or electrophiles

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nitrogen has a triple bond with a very large bond energy (944 kJ mol⁻¹), compared with the single Cl–Cl bond (242 kJ mol⁻¹). Breaking or weakening the N≡N bond needs a great deal of energy, so the activation energies of nitrogen's reactions are high. The bond is also non-polar, so the molecule does not attract electrophiles or nucleophiles. Chlorine's weak bond breaks easily, so chlorine is very reactive.

explanation: Strong, non-polar triple bond → high activation energy.
hints: Compare the bond energies and think about activation energy.

stem: Explain why phosphorus can form PCl₅ but nitrogen cannot form NCl₅.

points.description: Phosphorus (Period 3) has vacant 3d orbitals / can have more than eight outer electrons
Nitrogen (Period 2) has no d orbitals in its outer shell, so it can have at most eight outer electrons (four pairs)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Phosphorus is in Period 3 and can use its empty 3d orbitals to hold more than eight electrons, so it forms five bonds. Nitrogen's outer shell (n = 2) has only s and p orbitals, so it is limited to eight electrons and cannot form five bonds.

explanation: Expanded octets need an outer shell with d orbitals (Period 3 onwards).
hints: Which shell are the outer electrons in?

stem: Bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹, data booklet): H–F 562, H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe and explain the trend in the H–X bond energy down Group 17.

points.description: Bond energy decreases from H–F to H–I
The halogen atom gets larger, so the bond is longer and the shared pair is further from (and more shielded from) the halogen nucleus, so it is attracted less strongly

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The bond energy falls from 562 to 299 kJ mol⁻¹ because the halogen atoms get larger: the bond gets longer and the shared pair is further from the halogen nucleus and more shielded, so it is held less strongly.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which hydrogen halide is most easily split into its atoms by heating?

options.rationale: HF has the strongest bond.
HCl has the second strongest bond.
H–Br is stronger than H–I.
Correct: it has the weakest bond.

parts.explanation: The weakest bond (H–I, 299 kJ mol⁻¹) breaks most easily; a hot wire dipped into HI gives violet iodine vapour.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the difference, in kJ mol⁻¹, between the H–Cl and H–Br bond energies.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of hydrogen chloride (outer electrons only).

points.description: One shared pair (one dot from H, one cross from Cl) between H and Cl
Three lone pairs on chlorine (six crosses)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: H and Cl share one pair (one electron from each atom). Chlorine also has three lone pairs, so it has eight outer electrons; hydrogen has two.

explanation: Bond energies fall down the group as bonds lengthen; H–I is the easiest to break.
hints: Link bond length to atomic size.

stem: Aluminium chloride sublimes at about 180 °C. In the vapour at this temperature it exists mainly as Al₂Cl₆ molecules.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many outer electrons does an aluminium atom have in a single AlCl₃ molecule (counting shared electrons)?
parts.explanation: Three Al–Cl bonding pairs: six electrons.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Three Al–Cl bonding pairs: six electrons.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe how two AlCl₃ molecules join to form Al₂Cl₆.

points.description: A chlorine atom in one AlCl₃ donates a lone pair to the aluminium of the other
This happens twice / two coordinate (dative) bonds form
Each aluminium then has eight outer electrons (four chlorine atoms around it)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In each AlCl₃ the aluminium has only six outer electrons. A chlorine atom of one molecule donates a lone pair to the aluminium of the other, and a chlorine of the second molecule does the same in return, forming two coordinate bonds. Each aluminium then has an octet and four chlorine neighbours.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the type of bond formed between the two AlCl₃ units.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why aluminium chloride has a much lower melting (sublimation) point than aluminium oxide.

points.description: Aluminium chloride is covalent / simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces, whereas aluminium oxide is a giant ionic lattice with strong ionic bonds

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Aluminium chloride consists of covalent molecules held by weak intermolecular forces, whereas aluminium oxide is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attractions.

explanation: Electron-deficient Al accepts lone pairs from bridging Cl atoms: two dative bonds in Al₂Cl₆.
